title: Lav 2
hook: the second round: the Guru leads you to the fearless One, and ego's filth is gone (Suhi M4, ang 773)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first lav, and your line: round one: dharma. Did you do one plain duty slowly, as if it were part of a ceremony? The couple has bowed and sat down. The granthi opens to the second stanza. Day six hundred sixty-three.

Ask anyone who's been married a while what scared them on the wedding day, and the answers are honest. Will this last? Am I enough? What will his mother think? What if we turn into our parents? Weddings are full of fear dressed up in flowers. Under the music, two people are stepping into something they can't fully see. So it's striking that the second round of the Sikh wedding, sung while the couple walks, is about fear, and about leaving it behind. Today: lav two.
screen: `WILL THIS LAST? AM I ENOUGH?` → `FEAR DRESSED IN FLOWERS.` → `A ROUND ABOUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: The second stanza of Guru Ram Das's laavan, still on Ang seven seventy-three, says, in paraphrase: in the second round, the Lord leads you to meet the true Guru. The heart takes on the fear of God, and the filth of ego is washed away. Singing the Lord's praises, you see the Lord everywhere, and the unstruck music sounds within. Two kinds of fear meet in that stanza, and the difference matters. One is the fear that shrinks you: what will people say, will I fail, what if I'm left. The other, in Gurbani's language, is bhau, a reverent awe of God, the way you feel at the edge of an ocean. Sikh teachers say the second kind cures the first. When you stand in awe of the One, the smaller fears lose their grip. That's why the stanza leads toward the nirbhau, the Fearless One. You've met that word before: it's in the Mul Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, among the first things said about God. Ego is the other thing round two names. Haumai, the I that wants to win the argument, keep score, be right. The stanza calls it filth, and says it's washed off. For a couple, that's practical: a marriage where both people stop keeping score is a different marriage. For a soul, it's the next step after duty: once you're walking the path, the path starts to clean you. Then a lovely detail. The stanza says the unstruck sound, the anahad, plays inside. A music no one is playing. Round two ends listening.
screen: `ROUND TWO: TO MEET THE TRUE GURU.` · `TWO FEARS: THE SMALL ONE AND AWE.` · `NIRBHAU: THE FEARLESS ONE.` · `EGO WASHED OFF, MUSIC WITHIN.` · then, large: `ROUND TWO: FEARLESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one slow circle again. Stand if you can, and walk a small clockwise round, or trace one with your hand. This time bring along one small fear you're carrying today. Name it plainly. Halfway around, let your attention widen: to the room, the sky outside, how much bigger the world is than the fear. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you complete the round. Then sit, and listen to whatever sound is there. The bell holds the time.
Lav two. The second round of the Sikh wedding: led to the true Guru, awe of God replaces the small fears, ego's filth washes away, and an unstruck music plays within.
Your line: round two: fearless. Today, when a small fear shows up, notice it, and then notice something bigger and older than it. Day six hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: At the Anand Karaj, the second of Guru Ram Das's four laavan is read and then sung while the couple walks a second time around the Guru Granth Sahib.

what a scholar hears: Gurbani pairs bhau, reverent fear, with nirbhau, the Fearless One: the right fear frees you from every other.
